title: The Away Day That Finishes at Lunch
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that the full-day team away day is mostly wasted time and offers a complete half-day agenda for setting a team's priorities for the coming year. He starts from a survey finding that work occupied only 36% of the time on company offsites and illustrates the problem with a team of 14 that spent seven hours, 98 person-hours in all, and left with 11 priorities nobody could later name. His fix is the One Outcome Per Hour rule: decide what each hour must produce and stop when you have it. The five steps run from 9:00 to 12:30 and move from individual written answers, through a shared picture of next year and a dot vote for three priorities, to owners and first 30-day steps for each. He adds scripts to say aloud, a no-slides rule for the leader, and advice on what to do when the venue is already booked for the full day or three priorities feels too few.
points: Time and not content is the usual flaw in away days: a room booked for a day gets an agenda built to fill it, so match the schedule to the number of outcomes needed (three outcomes, three hours).
Have the team write their answers before the leader speaks and replace the strategy deck with a one-page summary sent a week ahead.
Starting from a vivid picture of next year, such as an intranet headline, keeps the group on what it wants rather than on last year's complaints.
End with three priorities, a 'not this year' list, an owner and a 30-day first step for each, and never shortchange the owner step, because a priority without an owner does not get done.
quotes: The report’s headline finding is that the most effective offsites are getting shorter.
That day cost 14 people 7 hours each: 98 person-hours, plus the room.
The room was booked for a day, so the agenda was built to fill it.
The first thing on the wall is the team’s thinking. Everyone writes before the leader says a word.
Starting from next year keeps you focussed on what the team wants. Looking back first tends to fill the hour with what went wrong last year.
Never take from step 4: a priority that leaves the room without an owner doesn’t get done.
Avoid filling it with more breakouts. The priorities are set by lunchtime, and more discussion in the afternoon tends to reopen them.
Three is what the team commits to together. Everyone’s day-to-day work carries on alongside them.
